summary: Examines how the Path Computation Element architecture, protocols, and extensions apply to computing paths that cross multiple areas or autonomous systems in MPLS and GMPLS traffic-engineered networks.

eli5.summary: When a trip crosses regions managed by different groups, a planner can help find the route. This looks at how well that works.

questions: how does pce compute paths across autonomous systems
what is backward recursive pce computation
subtitle: Extends path computation across multiple network areas and domains.

tldr.problem: Computing paths across multiple network domains requires finding routes when no single node has visibility of the entire topology, and domains often keep their internal structure confidential.
tldr.mechanism: The PCE (Path Computation Element) architecture uses per-domain path computation, backward recursive PCE procedures, and hierarchical PCE to cooperatively compute end-to-end paths across multi-area and multi-AS networks.
tldr.outcome: Enables traffic engineering in large networks by allowing PCEs in different domains to cooperate on path computation while maintaining topology confidentiality.

today: RFC 8694 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary applicability statement for PCE in multi-domain and multi-area networks.

sections.title: Multi-Domain Path Computation
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture, defined in RFC 4655, provides a framework for computing paths across networks that span multiple areas or autonomous systems. Computing end-to-end paths across multi-domain environments is complex because no single node may have full visibility of the topology across domain boundaries, and domains often hide their internal structure for confidentiality, scalability, or policy reasons.

This document examines how the PCE architecture applies to computing paths in MPLS and GMPLS traffic-engineered networks that cross multiple IGP areas or autonomous systems. It covers the applicability of PCE mechanisms, deployment options, and considerations for making multi-domain path computation practical.
sections.eli5: When a trip crosses regions managed by different groups, you need the groups to work together to plan the route without each revealing their internal roads.

sections.title: PCE Architecture and Mechanisms
sections.content:
The PCE uses several mechanisms to compute multi-domain paths. Per-domain path computation (RFC 5152) works when the sequence of domains is known in advance: each PCE computes its segment based on constraints, and the path is stitched together. The Backward Recursive PCE-based Computation (BRPC) procedure (RFC 5441) improves this by computing paths recursively from destination to source, selecting the optimal domain sequence along the way.

For more complex deployments, Hierarchical PCE (H-PCE) (RFC 6805) introduces parent PCEs that can discover intra-domain paths and determine the optimal end-to-end domain sequence without requiring the domain order to be known in advance. The choice of mechanism depends on whether the domain sequence is known, whether inter-AS-capable PCEs can discover each other, and what objective functions (optimality criteria) apply.
sections.eli5: PCEs can compute a path if they know the regions to cross (per-domain), figure out the best regions to cross by working backward (BRPC), or have a parent planner coordinate across all regions (Hierarchical PCE).

sections.title: Domain Structure and Constraints
sections.content:
A domain is a separate administrative, geographic, or switching environment with its own address management and path computation responsibility. Domains may be IGP areas or autonomous systems. In GMPLS networks, domains can be routing areas or subnetworks in an ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Network).

Multi-domain path computation must handle several considerations: networks may have multiple interconnect points (multihoming) where paths can enter or exit a domain; operators may need to include or exclude specific domains or autonomous systems from the path; synchronized path computations may be needed for dependent requests (e.g., primary and backup paths must be disjoint); and the operator may want paths that share ingress and egress domains but avoid transiting common intermediate domains.
sections.eli5: Different regions have different sizes and multiple roads between them. The planner must consider where paths can cross, whether to use certain regions, and how to keep primary and backup routes separate.

sections.title: Inter-Area Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
In IGP hierarchies with multiple areas, the flooding of topology information is limited to within area boundaries for scalability. An Area Border Router (ABR) connects areas. Without PCEs, inter-area paths are computed using per-domain path computation based on loose hops and Explicit Route Object (ERO) expansion at each ABR; this does not guarantee optimal paths and may require multiple crankback messages if the computed path is not feasible.

PCE-based inter-area path computation resolves this by introducing path computation entities that can cooperate across area boundaries. The BRPC method allows operators to specify which ABRs must be included or excluded from inter-area paths. Paths can be strictly explicit (a sequence of specific hops) or loose (e.g., a list of ABRs). PCEs can also compute diverse paths across areas, ensuring that primary and backup paths are disjoint at the link, node, or SRLG level.
sections.eli5: Within a large region split into smaller areas, path planners at the area borders can work together to find paths that cross area boundaries reliably and pick alternative routes when needed.

sections.title: Inter-AS Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
Inter-AS LSPs traverse multiple autonomous systems, each typically administered separately. Like inter-area path computation, inter-AS computation benefits from PCE cooperation. ASes are typically separated by AS Border Routers (ASBRs). Operators may need to include or exclude specific ASes, ensure bandwidth guarantees across the AS boundary (important for Diffserv and QoS services), provide recovery mechanisms (1+1 protection or m:n protection for groups of LSPs), and enforce peering policies.

Unlike inter-area networks within a single provider, inter-AS networks often involve separate service providers with formal peering agreements. PCE peering policies must enforce these agreements, similar to how BGP peering policies work. Multiple PCEs deployed in different ASes cooperate using BRPC, and the network topology database synchronization becomes critical; BGP-LS can distribute link-state and traffic engineering information between ASes for use by parent PCEs.
sections.eli5: When paths cross separate company networks, each company's path planner must follow its agreements with the other companies while still computing good paths together.

sections.title: Deployment and Domain Confidentiality
sections.content:
PCE deployment requires each PCE to maintain a Traffic Engineering Database (TED) of its domain's topology and resource information. The TED may be fed by IGP extensions (OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE) or by BGP-LS. In multi-domain deployments, maintaining topology information across domains is complex: flooding full topology information breaks confidentiality and does not scale; PCEs preserve confidentiality by returning paths with loose hops (where downstream PCEs expand the hops) or by using Path-Keys (tokens that hide explicit path segments).

Pre-planning and management-based approaches can supplement dynamic path computation: offline path computation by management systems is appropriate for long-lived LSPs in transport networks. Policy frameworks allow each PCC to select which PCEs to use, each PCE to control which PCEs it trusts for information, and each entity to define which objective functions apply to path computation.
sections.eli5: To protect private network information, each region's path planner shares only loose directions ("go toward this border") or encrypted path hints (Path-Keys) rather than every internal road.
